events.text: The well in the town square starts running backwards. Not drying up: running backwards, the water climbing the rope and pooling on the lip and pouring up into the sky in a thin silver thread. The magistrate posts a guard on it. The guard asks to be posted elsewhere. Old women come at dusk to burn incense, and the smoke goes up the thread too.

choices.text: Climb down the well and look

effects.log: At the bottom the stones are dry and cold, and you hear, very far up, something drinking.

choices.text: Burn incense with the old women

effects.log: You burn incense with them. One of them tells you her grandmother saw this once, before a great war in heaven.

choices.text: Draw water elsewhere and say nothing

effects.log: You draw from the river. The river runs the right way, for now.

events.text: The crows have stopped talking. In every town along the road the crows sit on the roofs in rows, all facing the same way, and not one of them makes a sound. Beggars' Union runners say it is the same from the coast to the Western Regions. A fortune-teller at the crossroads has shut up his stall and gone home, which is the worst sign of all.

choices.text: Follow the way the crows are facing

effects.log: They face a point in the sky to the north-east. You find nothing there but cloud, and a cold that should not be in summer.

choices.text: Pay the Beggars' Union for every report of it

effects.log: The reports come in for a month. You have a map by the end, and an arrow on it, and you do not like where it points.

choices.text: Throw a stone and see if they scatter

effects.log: They do not scatter. The stone falls among them and they do not look at it.

events.text: A monk of Shaolin walks the length of the province ringing a hand-bell and saying nothing. When people stop him to ask, he shows them a slip of paper in the abbot's hand: the heavens are at war; do not be afraid; do not look up for long. Nobody is reassured. Everybody looks up.

choices.text: Walk a day with the monk

effects.log: He does not speak, but he shares his rice with you, and at night he weeps in his sleep.

choices.text: Ask the abbot what he knows

effects.log: The abbot says the old books tell of this. He will not say how the old books end.

choices.text: Look up for a long time anyway

effects.log: You look up until your neck aches. For a moment the blue seems thin, like paper held to a lamp.

events.text: The temple bells of the district ring by themselves at the third hour, every night, all at once, a single deep note. The monks have tied the clappers. The bells ring anyway. The note is the same in every temple, and it is not a note any of the bells were cast to make. Dogs howl at it. Babies sleep through it, which the mothers find worse.

choices.text: Sit in a temple at the third hour

effects.log: You sit under the bell when it rings. The note goes through you like cold water, and leaves something behind: a direction.

choices.text: Stuff your ears with wax and sleep

effects.log: You sleep. In the morning everyone else is grey with tiredness, and you are fresh, and a little ashamed.

choices.text: Pay a monk to ring against it, every night

effects.log: The monk rings a different note. The two notes fight in the dark. Yours wins, some nights.

events.text: At noon on a clear day, every person in the market has two shadows: their own, and a second one, fainter, falling the wrong way, toward the sun. It lasts as long as it takes to drink a cup of tea. Then the second shadows go, all together, as if called. A child asks her mother where hers went. Her mother does not answer.

choices.text: Try to catch your second shadow

effects.log: You stamp on it. It slides out from under your foot like a fish, and for a moment you feel it look at you.

choices.text: Help the stall-keepers calm the crowd

effects.log: You talk the market down. People finish their buying with shaking hands, and thank you.

choices.text: Go home and shut the shutters

effects.log: You shut them. In the dim room you have one shadow, and you watch it all afternoon.

events.text: Snow falls in midsummer over the southern hills, and it is grey. It does not melt. It lies in the paddies like ash, and the rice under it does not die but stops growing, as if it had forgotten what it was for. The farmers sweep it into heaps. The heaps are cold to the touch even at noon, and hum faintly when the wind is still.

choices.text: Help sweep the paddies clean

effects.log: You sweep a whole village's paddies with your qi. The rice starts again, slowly, unsure.

choices.text: Take a jar of the snow to an alchemist

effects.log: The alchemist will not open the jar in the house. Outside, she says it is not of this world at all.

choices.text: Buy up rice before the price climbs

effects.log: You buy early. The price climbs. You are richer, and the village knows why.

events.text: An old storyteller in the tea-house tells a story you have never heard: of a sky that cracked once, long ago, and a cold thing that looked through the crack at the world the way a man looks at a meal. It was driven off by the gods, she says. She tells it badly, distracted. She keeps looking at the ceiling.

choices.text: Ask her where she heard it

effects.log: From her grandmother, who heard it from a monk, who heard it in a dream. She is not sure it is a story at all.

choices.text: Buy her a cup, and ask for the ending

effects.log: The ending, she says, is that the gods win. She says it the way people say a prayer.

choices.text: Leave before she finishes

effects.log: You leave. Outside, you find you are looking at the sky too.

events.text: The Tang family's poisons have gone flat. The Wudang's talismans curl at the edges. Every master alchemist in the Central Plains is complaining that their furnaces burn grey at the heart. It is as if the whole martial world had caught a cold. Elders who remember nothing like it are writing to elders who remember less.

choices.text: Test your own arts against it

effects.log: Your qi is a little thinner, a little harder to call. You train twice as hard and keep level.

choices.text: Write to the old masters for what they know

effects.log: One of them writes back: 'Look up. It is not us. It is above.' You keep the letter.

choices.text: Sell what talismans you have while they work

effects.log: You sell them quickly at a good price. Your buyers find out within a month.

events.text: The sky goes wrong at dusk. Not dark, not stormy: wrong. The blue turns the colour of a bruise healing backwards, and the first stars come out in the wrong places, in shapes no astrologer has a name for. Across the town people stop in the street, bowls in hand, and look up. Nobody speaks. A dog sits down in the road.

choices.text: Climb to the highest roof and watch

effects.log: You watch the wrong stars until dawn puts them out. You remember every shape. They will come in useful.

choices.text: Go round the houses calming people

effects.log: You knock on doors until midnight. People are glad of a face, any face.

choices.text: Light every lamp in your house

effects.log: Your house blazes like a lantern. The neighbours come and sit in your yard, near the light.

events.text: There is a seam in the sky over the Central Plains, running from horizon to horizon, thin and grey like a scar on a face. It was not there last week. Martial artists from every sect have climbed every peak to look at it. The bravest say it is moving, very slowly, like a sleeper turning over, and that something on the other side is awake.

choices.text: Climb Mount Hua to see it close

effects.log: From the summit you see the seam breathe. Once, for a moment, it opens a crack, and you see a grey you will never forget.

choices.text: Gather with the masters at the foot of the peaks

effects.log: The masters argue for three days. For the first time in a century, nobody draws a sword on anyone.

choices.text: Keep your eyes on the road

effects.log: You keep them on the road. It is a good road, and it does not crack.

events.text: The sun comes up grey. It is the same sun, the right size, in the right place, but it has lost its colour, like a coin rubbed smooth. It gives light and very little warmth. The farmers go out to the fields anyway. Monks chant on every hill. Somewhere in the province, a scholar of the heavens has hanged a bell at the city gate to ring every hour the sun stays grey.

choices.text: Meditate in the grey light

effects.log: The grey light makes your qi move strangely, cold and sharp. You learn something from it, unwillingly.

choices.text: Work the fields with the farmers

effects.log: You work beside them all day. By evening the sun has warmed a little, and so have you.

choices.text: Count the bell, and wait

effects.log: The bell rings eleven times. On the twelfth hour, the sun is gold again. You let out a breath you held all day.

events.text: The moon has a crack in it. Everyone can see it: a thin black line across its face, from top to bottom, like a dropped plate mended badly. On the second night, light leaks out of the crack, a light that is not moonlight, and where it falls on the river, the fish come up to the surface and stare.

choices.text: Catch the strange light in a bowl

effects.log: It sits in the bowl like milk, and is gone by dawn, and the bowl is cold for a year.

choices.text: Keep the children indoors after dark

effects.log: You talk the whole street into it. No child of the street goes out under that moon.

choices.text: Sit by the river and watch the fish

effects.log: The fish watch you back. Toward dawn they sink, one by one, as if they had seen enough.

events.text: Colour drains from the world at dusk, every dusk, for a week: red first, then gold, then green, until the whole town is the shade of old ink. When the sun rises the colours come back, a little paler each time. The dyers' guild has closed. A painter in the next street has started painting only at night, by lamplight, in colours nobody else can see.

choices.text: Sit with the painter through a night

effects.log: His paintings are full of red. You look at them till dawn, and the red stays with you.

choices.text: Go out into the grey, and walk in it

effects.log: You walk through a town of ink. Every face you pass is frightened. You smile at all of them.

choices.text: Buy up all the dye that is left

effects.log: You buy it cheap. When the colours come back, it sells dear. Someone has to.

events.text: The whole sky shakes. Not thunder: the sky itself, the blue of it, shudders like a drumskin, once, twice, a third time, and every bird in the province goes up at once and does not come down for an hour. Martial artists stand in their courtyards with swords drawn at nothing. Far above, something is hitting the heavens from the other side.

choices.text: Draw your own sword, and stand ready

effects.log: You stand ready until dusk. Nothing comes down. Your arm aches, and your heart is steady.

choices.text: Pray to the gods above to hold

effects.log: You pray. You do not know if they hear. The shuddering stops before the fourth blow.

choices.text: Run for the hills

effects.log: You run. The sky does not follow. You come back in a week, sheepish, to find others did the same.

events.text: A hole opens in the sky over the town at noon, round as a well-mouth and grey inside, and things come down out of it on threads, like spiders. They are the size of a man and the shape of a memory of one. Where they touch the ground, the cobbles go soft. The town guard runs. The magistrate runs. Somebody has to decide.

choices.text: Hold the square, and cut the threads

ok.log: You cut thread after thread. The hole above narrows, then shrinks, then closes like an eye. The town stands.

fail.log: There are too many threads. You are driven back to the river and the square goes grey behind you.

choices.text: Flee with the townsfolk to the hills

effects.log: You take the old and the slow and get them to the hills. Behind you, the town goes quiet.

events.text: The sky tears over the mountain pass as your caravan is halfway through. Grey pours down the slopes like smoke, and in the smoke there are shapes walking, slow and certain. The muleteers are already turning the beasts. The merchant you are guarding clutches your sleeve and says nothing at all, because there is nothing worth saying.

choices.text: Hold the pass while the caravan turns

ok.log: You hold the narrowest part of the pass until the last mule is clear. The grey stops at your feet as if at a line.

fail.log: You hold for an hour. Then the walkers are past you, and you are running with the mules, and half the goods are lost.

choices.text: Turn and run with the mules

effects.log: You run. The caravan comes out the far end of the valley with all its mules and none of its pride.

events.text: In the middle of a sect's great courtyard, during the morning drills, the air splits like silk. A cold breath comes out, and then a hand, grey and very long, feeling about the flagstones as if looking for something it had dropped. The disciples scatter. The elders stand frozen. You are the nearest blade.

choices.text: Strike the hand before it finds its grip

ok.log: Your blade bites. The hand goes back through the split, and the split closes on it with a sound like a slammed door.

fail.log: Your blade bites, and the hand does not care. It sweeps you across the courtyard. The split widens before the elders move.

choices.text: Get the young disciples out the back gate

effects.log: You herd them out. The elders hold the courtyard behind you as long as elders can.

events.text: The river stops. Upstream, a grey light has come down out of the sky and stands in the water like a pillar, and the river parts around it and will not flow past. On the far bank, a village is waking up to find its fields drying in an hour. Something is coming down the pillar, slowly, the way a man comes down a ladder.

choices.text: Wade out and meet it at the foot of the pillar

ok.log: You meet it at the foot. It does not reach the ground. The pillar fades, and the river runs on, muddy and loud.

fail.log: It reaches the ground. You are thrown into the river and carried a mile, and the village empties behind you.

choices.text: Get the village across the dry bed while you can

effects.log: You lead them across the dry bed before the river comes back. The village is gone, and the people are not.

events.text: The tear comes at night, over the inn where you are sleeping. You wake to a silence so total that you cannot hear your own breath, and out of the window the stars are gone, and a grey shape is standing in the yard, looking up at the windows one by one, counting them. It reaches yours. It smiles, if that is the word.

choices.text: Go down and face it in the yard

ok.log: You go down. It stops counting. You fight in perfect silence, and when it breaks the stars come back all at once.

fail.log: You go down. It does not stop counting while it fights you. You lose, and the inn is grey by morning.

choices.text: Wake the inn and run out the back

effects.log: You wake them all and run out the back into the dark. The thing keeps counting empty windows.

events.text: The breach opens over a great clan's manor during a wedding feast. The bride is still at the gate. Grey ribbons come down out of the sky like a second set of decorations, and wherever they touch, a lantern goes out and a guest forgets their own name. The groom has drawn his sword and does not know which way to point it.

choices.text: Stand with the groom and hold the gate

ok.log: You and the groom cut the ribbons till the sky closes. The bride walks through the gate after all, a little late.

fail.log: The ribbons are too many. You get the bride out over the wall, and the manor is grey behind you.

choices.text: Carry the bride and the old ones out the side gate

effects.log: You get them out the side gate. The groom holds the front for as long as he can, and lives, barely.

events.text: A tear opens over the market at Luoyang, and the grey that comes down is hungry in a way you can feel on your skin. Stalls go colourless. Coins go cold. The crowds break and run in every direction at once. In the middle of the square, a child is sitting on an upturned basket, quite still, looking up at the tear with interest.

choices.text: Stand over the child and hold

ok.log: You stand over the child till the tear closes. The child asks if you will do it again. You say no.

fail.log: The grey is too strong. You snatch the child up and break out of the square with your qi in tatters.

choices.text: Grab the child and run with the crowd

effects.log: You run with the child under your arm. Behind you the market is grey, and ahead the crowd is screaming, and you are both alive.

events.text: The sky opens over the training ground where you are teaching a dozen young students their first stances. A grey thing steps out of the air as if through a doorway, and looks at the students the way a fox looks at a henhouse. The students turn to you as one. You have taught them for a year that a martial artist does not run.

choices.text: Show them a martial artist does not run

ok.log: You hold it until it goes. The students will never forget it, and none of them will ever run.

fail.log: You hold it as long as you can, and then you shout at them to run, and they do, and so, in the end, do you.

choices.text: Teach them the second lesson: when to run

effects.log: You run with them. They are angry with you for a month, and alive to be angry.

events.text: The breach is closed. Where the grey came down, the ground is pale and cold and will grow nothing for a season. The town comes out of its houses slowly, then all at once, and stands round the spot in a ring. An old woman brings you a bowl of noodles and presses it into your hands. Nobody says much. Somebody starts to laugh, and cannot stop.

choices.text: Eat the noodles, sitting in the square

effects.log: You eat them in the square. Children sit round you and watch every mouthful. It is very good.

choices.text: Walk the edge of the grey ground and fix it in memory

effects.log: You walk the edge. You will know this shape again if it comes back. It does not.

events.text: Word of what you did at the breach has gone ahead of you. In the next town the innkeeper will not take your money. In the one after, the magistrate bows. A storyteller in Kaifeng has already got most of it wrong, and has made you taller. Martial artists you have never met write asking you to teach them how you held.

choices.text: Write back to them all

effects.log: It takes a winter. Some of your letters are wise. A few are only honest.

choices.text: Correct the storyteller about your height

effects.log: He listens, nods, and makes you taller still. The crowd loves it.

events.text: In the nights after the breach, you dream of the grey. In the dream it is not angry. It is hungry in a cold, polite way, like a guest who has been kept waiting at a feast. You wake with your fists clenched and your qi up. The physician says it will pass. A monk says it will not pass, but you will learn to sleep beside it.

choices.text: Learn the monk's way of sleeping

effects.log: It takes a year. You sleep. On the worst nights you are still glad you held.

choices.text: Train through the nights instead

effects.log: You train until your body forgets the dream. Your strength grows. So does the tiredness.

events.text: A great sect sends an elder to your door with a gift and a question. They have heard you held a breach, and they want to know how it fought, what it feared, how the sky closed. They are writing it all down, the elder says, in a book for the next time. He says 'the next time' quite simply, the way a farmer says 'next winter'.

choices.text: Tell him everything, slowly

effects.log: He writes for two days. Years later, someone you will never meet reads it and lives.

choices.text: Tell him, and ask for a manual in return

effects.log: He laughs and agrees. The manual is old and good.

events.text: You fled the breach, and you are alive, and the people you led out are alive. That is the truth of it. In the camp in the hills, around a cold fire, nobody blames you. The grey has not followed. Below, the town you left is quiet in a way towns never are, and you can see it from the ridge every morning.

choices.text: Go back down to see what is left

effects.log: Most of it is there, grey and hushed and empty. You bring back a few things for those who asked.

choices.text: Look after the camp, and do not look down

effects.log: You keep the fire going and the children fed. It is enough to do, and it has to be.

events.text: Some people in the martial world call you a coward now, quietly, behind their sleeves. You fled the breach when others held. The others who held are mostly dead, which the sleeves do not mention. An old master you respect stops you in the street, looks you over carefully, and says: 'Good. Now be useful.'

choices.text: Be useful: help the towns that held

effects.log: You spend a year carting rice to the grey towns. People stop whispering, not because of you, but because they are tired.

choices.text: Train in secret, so next time you can hold

effects.log: You train every night. Next time, you tell yourself. Next time.

events.text: The people you got out of the breach have settled in a valley a day's walk from where they lived. They have built a few houses and named the place after their old town, with one word added: New. The head of the households asks you to stay a while, and help them find their feet. Their old shrine is lost, and they want you to bless the new one.

choices.text: Stay, and bless the shrine

effects.log: You bless it badly, never having done it. They are delighted. The shrine stands, and is visited.

choices.text: Give them silver for the building, and go

effects.log: You leave what silver you can. They name a beam after you.

events.text: Months after you fled, you still wake at night with the grey in your mouth. You ran, and you would run again, and the knowing does not help. A wandering monk you share a fire with listens to all of it and then says that running is also a choice, and the people you ran with would agree. He offers you the last of his tea.

choices.text: Drink the tea, and sleep

effects.log: You sleep the whole night through, for the first time since.

choices.text: Ask him how to forgive yourself

effects.log: He says you do not. You just go on, and one day you notice you have. It sounds like nonsense. It turns out true.

events.text: The sky over the world has been wrong for longer than anyone alive remembers. The seam across it is old now, grey, and the stars along its edge come out in the wrong places every night. Children are born under it and think nothing of it. Old people still glance up at dusk, out of habit, the way people check a door they know is locked.

choices.text: Learn the wrong stars by heart

effects.log: You learn them all. They are a map of something. You do not yet know what.

choices.text: Teach a child the right stars, from the old books

effects.log: You teach her the old sky. She listens as if to a fairy tale, and then asks why it went away.

choices.text: Never look up at all

effects.log: You never look up. You are calmer than most people. You miss a good many things.

events.text: Every year, a little grey comes down through the seam in the sky. It comes as snow, or as rain, or as a fog in the low valleys that makes people forget the names of their neighbours. The sects take turns to burn it away with their qi. This year it is the turn of a sect too small to manage, and the valley under it is waiting.

choices.text: Go and help the small sect

effects.log: You burn grey for a month beside strangers. They are poor, and very grateful, and very good at it.

choices.text: Ask the great sects to send help

effects.log: You carry letters for a month. Two great sects send help, late, and grumble.

choices.text: Stay out of other sects' business

effects.log: You stay out. The valley forgets its neighbours' names that winter, and remembers yours.

events.text: The martial world has a new kind of master now: the grey-walkers, who go into the places where the sky came down and bring out what can be brought. They are odd people, quiet and a little pale, and they are paid well. One of them sits at your table in the tea-house and asks if you would like to learn their trade.

choices.text: Learn the trade

effects.log: You walk the grey with them for a year. You come out paler, richer and much quieter.

choices.text: Ask what they have found in there

effects.log: Things from other worlds, they say. Coins, toys, a letter in no language. They never sell the letters.

choices.text: Decline politely

effects.log: They nod. They are used to it. They pay for your tea anyway.

events.text: A temple has been built at the foot of the place where the sky first came down, long ago. Monks keep a flame there that has not gone out in centuries, and every pilgrim who passes adds a stick of wood. It is said that if the flame ever goes out, the seam will open all the way. Nobody believes this. Nobody lets the flame go out.

choices.text: Add a stick, and kneel

effects.log: You add your stick and kneel a while. The heat of it is ordinary, and good.

choices.text: Stay a season and tend the flame

effects.log: You tend it through a bitter winter, when the monks are sick. It does not go out.

choices.text: Ask the monks what is really under it

effects.log: They tell you, in the end: nothing. It is only a flame. That is the point of it.

events.text: The farmers of the plains have learned to plant by the wrong stars. The old almanacs are useless now; the new ones are written by blind astrologers who go by the feel of the cold. The harvests are thinner than in the old songs, but they come. At the autumn fair, a farmer shows you a rice-ear grown under the grey and says it tastes of nothing, but it fills a bowl.

choices.text: Buy a sack, and eat it

effects.log: It does taste of nothing. It fills the bowl. You eat it every day that winter.

choices.text: Bring the farmer a good almanac from the old days

effects.log: He reads it with great sorrow, and then plants by it, half his field. That half does better.

choices.text: Ask the blind astrologers how they see

effects.log: They say they listen to the cold. They let you try. You hear nothing, then something.

events.text: A rumour runs along the river: the sky is mending. Somebody's grandmother saw a star come back to its right place last spring, and the seam is a finger narrower than it was. The scholars say it is nonsense. The fishermen say it is true. Everybody you meet looks up more often now, the way people look at a sick friend who has eaten a little soup.

choices.text: Climb a hill and measure the seam

effects.log: You measure it with a rod and a candle for a year. It is narrower. Only a hair. A hair is something.

choices.text: Spread the rumour, true or not

effects.log: You spread it. People smile more that year. That is not nothing either.

choices.text: Keep your hopes where they belong

effects.log: You keep them low. They are safer there, and duller.

events.text: A stranger has been following you from town to town: tall, courteous, with a face that never quite settles when you look straight at it. It never comes close. It is always at the far end of the market, or the far side of the river. When you finally turn and walk toward it, it bows to you, very low, like a guest to a host who has kept it waiting a long time.

choices.text: Draw on it before it straightens

ok.log: It does not straighten. It goes to grey smoke under your blade and leaves a smell like a cold star.

fail.log: It straightens. It looks at you, quite sadly, and says it was mistaken: you are not the one yet. Then it strikes.

choices.text: Bow back, and take another road

effects.log: You bow back and take the east road. It does not follow, this time.

events.text: The fortune-teller at the crossroads grabs your wrist as you pass and will not let go. She says a thing is looking for you that has looked for you through many lives. It lost its whole heaven to you once, she says, and it has never stopped being hungry about it. She lets go, and asks for three coppers, and is crying.

choices.text: Pay her far more than three coppers

effects.log: You give her a whole string. She stops crying, and gives you a charm to sleep with.

choices.text: Ask her how to hide from it

effects.log: She says: be unremarkable. It hunts greatness. You find this difficult advice.

choices.text: Laugh, and walk on

effects.log: You laugh. That night, on the inn roof, something walks back and forth until dawn.

events.text: Someone has been killing the strongest masters in the province, one by one, and leaving them unharmed: alive, and grey, and empty of their qi, as if something had drunk it. The martial world is in an uproar. The last master to fall whispered one thing to the physicians before he went quiet: it was asking for someone else. It was asking for you.

choices.text: Go to the place it struck last, and wait

effects.log: You wait a week. It does not come. You think, on the last night, that it was there, and decided not to.

choices.text: Hide your strength under a beggar's rags

effects.log: You live as a beggar for a year. Nobody grey comes asking. You learn a great deal about beggars.

choices.text: Call on the sects to hunt it together

effects.log: They hunt it for a season. They never catch it. It stops, which may be the same thing.

events.text: In a dream you stand on a battlefield at the edge of heaven, holding a broken sun, and a god with no face kneels in front of you and says your name. You wake. The name is not your name in this life. But at the foot of your bed, on the floor, there are grey footprints that lead to the window and stop.

choices.text: Follow the prints, as far as they go

effects.log: They go up the wall and onto the roof and stop at the edge, as if whatever left them stepped up into the sky.

choices.text: Scrub them out before anyone sees

effects.log: You scrub them out. They come up white, then gone. You are careful, after, to sleep with a lamp lit.

choices.text: Say the name from the dream aloud

effects.log: You say it. Something far away hears, and is afraid, and that is a strange thing to feel.

events.text: Every child in the martial world knows the story of the God Who Ended the Hunger: how the sky cracked, long ago, and a hungry thing from another world reached through, and a god of our heaven went to the end of everything and finished it. The story is told at festivals with paper lanterns and a great grey dragon that the children beat with sticks.

choices.text: Take a stick and beat the dragon

effects.log: You beat it with great energy. A child tells you that you are very good at it. You are.

choices.text: Tell the children a part they have never heard

effects.log: You tell them a detail you could not possibly know. They believe you at once, which is the best part.

events.text: In an old temple on a mountain you find a mural of the war in heaven: gods in a line against a grey sea, and at the front of them, one god with a broken sun in their hand. The paint has faded from that god's face. The monk who keeps the temple says it is the custom: the one who ended it chose to be reborn, and has no face so that anyone could be them.

choices.text: Look at the mural a long while

effects.log: You look until the monk brings you tea. You feel, foolishly, that the faded god is looking back.

choices.text: Leave an offering at its feet

effects.log: You leave a coin. The monk sees you do it, and bows to you, and does not say why.

events.text: The storytellers of the river towns have a saying: 'The sky remembers.' It means that the one who ended the Hunger long ago is still somewhere in the world, reborn and not knowing. When something good and unlikely happens, people say it. Today, when you pull a drowning boy from the river, the whole bank says it at once.

choices.text: Laugh, and wring out your sleeves

effects.log: You laugh. The boy's mother gives you a dry coat. The saying follows you all the way to the next town.

choices.text: Take it seriously for one quiet moment

effects.log: You stand on the bank and wonder. The river says nothing. The boy is fine.

events.text: A scholar of the heavens has written a book proving that the God Who Ended the Hunger was never real. It sells very well. You read it on a long journey. It is clever, and wrong, and you know it is wrong the way you would know if someone described your own house with the doors in the wrong places.

choices.text: Write to the scholar, politely, about the doors

effects.log: You write. The scholar writes back, puzzled and fascinated. The second edition is different.

choices.text: Leave the book on a bench for someone else

effects.log: You leave it. Someone will read it, and look up at the sky, which is the point either way.

events.text: On the anniversary of the Hunger's end, the whole martial world keeps a minute's silence at noon. Sects stop their drills, inns stop their noise, and even the bandits in the hills, it is said, lower their blades. You stand in the silence with everyone else. When it ends, an old beggar beside you says, 'Thank you,' to nobody in particular, and walks away.

choices.text: Go after the beggar

effects.log: You lose him in the crowd. For years you wonder what he saw in you.

choices.text: Say 'You are welcome' to the empty air

effects.log: You say it. It feels foolish and right at once. Someone nearby smiles.
